# How to Become a Top Contributor to an Open Source Project

URL: https://jcosta.tech/writing/top-oss-contributor/
Author: John Costa
Published: 2026-11-08

In April I wrote about [my first 100 merged open source PRs](https://jcosta.tech/writing/100-merged-prs-what-i-learned-contributing-to-open-source-with-ai/). Ink had 18 of them, and I was its third most active contributor.

It has 60 now. That makes me the second-largest contributor in the project's history, behind Sindre Sorhus and just ahead of Vadim Demedes, who created it. Ink is React for the terminal. It runs underneath Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Shopify's CLI, and it gets downloaded about 9.9 million times a week.

The path there is repeatable.

## Pick the reviewer first

The person reviewing your PRs decides whether they land. Look for a project where reviews happen within days, the maintainer explains what they want, and issues come with enough detail to reproduce.

oss-autopilot runs that search for me. It scores every repo on how likely a PR is to merge. It checks how active the project is, how fast maintainers review, how often outside PRs land, and whether someone already claimed the issue.

The first issue it surfaced for me was in Ink. I'd never used it. Everything I know about Ink I learned from inside the codebase, one issue at a time.

## Earn trust one small PR at a time

Sindre merged every one of my 60 PRs, and most landed with zero to three comments. That came from learning what he wants. He wants one change per PR, a test that fails without it, and a description that explains the mechanism.

The best descriptions read like a bug report followed by a proof. Show the input, what the main branch does with it, what it should do, and why your fix is the smallest correct one. When the reviewer can verify the claim from the description alone, the review goes to the design.

Small PRs earn the trust big ones need. My largest, kitty keyboard protocol support, ran about 1,700 lines and took many rounds of review. Sindre stuck with me through all of them.

Persistence matters as much as the code. A PR that goes a week without a reply or a rebase looks abandoned. oss-autopilot tracks every PR I have open and flags the ones waiting on me, which I covered in the April post.

## Turn review feedback into guardrails

Claude Code writes most of my code. I test and review every change before it goes up. Left alone, an agent repeats the mistakes every new contributor makes.

In April I said the goal was for maintainers never to give me the same feedback twice. prlore is how I got there. It mines a repo's PR history, pulls out the comments a maintainer makes again and again, checks them against the current code, and writes them up as a rulebook an agent can read. For Ink that came to about 200 rules from two years of reviews. The agent reads them before it writes code, and a review step checks every change against them before I open a PR.

The rulebook only works if something forces the lookup. Once we signed off on a change and Sindre broke it the same day. The rulebook already had a rule for exactly that shortcut. Checking it is now a required step. Every miss becomes a check.

Some rules went back upstream. A few of Sindre's most repeated comments were mechanical enough to test, so I added a check to Ink's test suite. The next contributor hears it from CI instead of from him.

## Widen your scope

Early on, everything I picked up was a bug someone else had reported. As I invested more in the project, I started finding my own work. I use Claude to audit the whole repo for edge cases nobody has filed yet. Many of my recent fixes came from those audits, including one that stopped a transform component from writing raw escape sequences straight to the terminal.

The same shift pulled me into upkeep. I added a weekly Windows run of the test suite. I answer questions in issues and discussions, triage new reports, and review other contributors' PRs.

Fixes help users. Upkeep helps the maintainer, whose time is the scarcest thing in any popular project.

Getting your first PR into a project is hard. Getting your sixtieth is a partnership.

[oss-autopilot](https://github.com/costajohnt/oss-autopilot) and [prlore](https://github.com/costajohnt/prlore) are open source, and everything that shipped in the latest Ink major is in the [8.0.0 release notes](https://github.com/vadimdemedes/ink/releases/tag/v8.0.0).

# I Bought Some Smart Bulbs and Ended Up With a Server Rack

URL: https://jcosta.tech/writing/from-smart-bulbs-to-a-server-rack/
Author: John Costa
Published: 2026-11-01

People ask what a homelab is, and the honest answer is that it's whatever happens after you buy one smart bulb and keep going. Mine grew one small decision at a time over many years, and looking back, each step followed from the limits of the one before it. This post walks through that path using my own setup as the case study, in the order it actually happened.

## Stage one: smart lights and a cheap speaker

For a lot of people the start is home automation, and that was true for me. Many years ago I wanted Hue lights so I could have smart lighting with fun colors, and an Amazon Echo was cheap enough that adding voice control hands free felt like an easy win.

From there the collection grows quietly. I added more lights, then more Echos around the apartment, then smart locks for the doors, then a security system with sensors on the windows, and then a handful of smart plugs so I could control whatever happened to be plugged into them.

That's when the first real problem shows up. Every one of those devices comes with its own app, its own login, and its own idea of how things should work. The Alexa app can pull a lot of it together, and for a while I used it as the bridge for as much as it could manage, but its interface is clunky and there's only so much you can do from it.

## Stage two: Homebridge and the first always-on computer

The next thing you hear about is Homebridge. It's software that runs on a Raspberry Pi or any small computer that stays on all the time, and it takes devices from all those separate vendor apps and brings them into Apple's Home app.

The Home app is genuinely nice, especially if you're on an iPhone, and it syncs across all your Apple devices. Its weakness is that relatively few smart devices pair with it natively, and Homebridge fills exactly that gap.

Having everything in one place also unlocks automations that cross vendors. Before, a Hue light and an Alexa smart plug lived in two different apps and had no way to talk to each other. With both in the Home app, a Hue light turning on can trigger the smart plug, and you can start building more complex automations from there.

The bigger change is quieter, though. Once you have a small computer running around the clock for Homebridge, you can run other software on it too. For me that was **Pi-hole**, which blocks ads for the whole network. A browser extension only protects the one browser it's installed in, while Pi-hole blocks ads for every device connected to your network, and that's where the name comes from.

## Stage three: Home Assistant on a mini PC

Eventually Homebridge runs out of road. Some devices still won't come into the Home app, and the automations you want get more complex than it handles well.

The next step up is **Home Assistant**, [an open source home automation platform](/writing/ai-assisted-home-automation-in-2026/). It can also connect to the Apple Home app, so Home Assistant becomes the central hub for every device and automation, and you choose which devices to pass through to the Home app. That split works well in our house. My wife can open the Home app on her iPhone and do the simple things like locking doors and turning lights on and off, while everything complicated lives in Home Assistant.

Home Assistant integrates with an enormous range of things. In our house it talks to the solar panels on the roof, a lot of smart plugs doing energy monitoring, cameras and the security system, a robot vacuum, and smart cat feeders, which adds up to over 100 devices. I also do presence detection over Bluetooth, which is a story on its own, because our two cats make traditional motion and presence sensors unreliable. You can get creative too. Cheap microcontroller boards like the ESP32 let you build your own sensors, and even something as small as a vibration sensor in the mailbox can send a notification to your phone when the mail arrives.

Home Assistant needs more compute than a Raspberry Pi comfortably gives it. There are dedicated devices sold for running it, which are small computers underneath, and a popular alternative is buying a small form factor desktop or a mini PC. You plug in a keyboard, mouse and monitor once to set it up, and after that you manage it remotely. What matters is that it stays on. That was my next step, with a mini PC running Home Assistant and Pi-hole.

## Stage four: self-hosting your subscriptions

Once you have a capable always-on machine, you start learning about self-hosted software, and there is a lot of free software out there that can [replace things you pay for every month](/writing/from-raspberry-pi-to-17-container-homelab/).

**Immich** handles photo storage and can stand in for Google Photos or iCloud. **Jellyfin** or **Plex** run a media server, so if you have a big collection of DVDs you can digitize them and stream them from anywhere, and share that library with friends and family. **Bitwarden** stores passwords and other sensitive credentials, and **Vaultwarden** is a lightweight server for it that you can host yourself, which is what I run. That list keeps going for a long time.

## Stage five: the lab part of homelab

If you like to tinker, or you're a software engineer like me, this is where the "lab" part kicks in. You might host your own web apps or websites, or learn networking. You might be building skills for your job as a software engineer, security engineer or IT professional, and a homelab is a safe place to build, deploy and manage containers, Kubernetes and the rest without breaking anything that matters at work.

In the AI era there's a newer reason too. With an always-on computer you can [run an AI assistant that's always available](/writing/always-on-claude-home-lab-node/), one you can message from anywhere and have it do things for you.

## Stage six: running out of compute

All of this adds up, and eventually you run low on something. Maybe it's RAM, maybe storage, maybe CPU, or maybe you start seeing thermal spikes. The answer at this stage is usually more hardware, so you buy another mini PC or two and spread your services across them.

## Stage seven: high availability

Then a different question shows up, which is how much you now depend on all of this. If the homelab goes down, can you still get into your house? Can you still reach your important data and your backups?

Once the answer starts to worry you, high availability matters. A common approach is to build a cluster of computers so there's redundancy built in. Each computer in the cluster is a node, and if any node goes down, another one can take over its work, so the system as a whole stays available.

At this point you basically have a small server rack, and you might organize your gear into an actual rack. You'll have networking gear too, starting with an Ethernet switch, which is a box full of Ethernet ports. Your internet connection plugs into the switch, and all your devices plug into it as well, so everything is on your wired network instead of depending on Wi-Fi. That's roughly where I am today.

## Stage eight: privacy and reliability

The stage I'm in now is about privacy and reliability. Even with everything managed in one place through Home Assistant, a lot of my devices still connect to their own vendor's cloud and send data back to the company that made them.

The robot vacuum is a good example, and it's the project I'm working on right now. Modern robot vacuums use LIDAR to map your home, and that map goes up to the manufacturer's servers, which means a company holds a detailed floor plan of your house. A video doorbell company might know who comes to your home and when.

So the next step is moving devices off the cloud and onto my local network only. Privacy is one benefit, and reliability is the other. If my internet goes out, or the vendor's service has an outage, nothing in my house changes, because as long as my own network is up, everything keeps working. I'm doing that by moving Wi-Fi devices over to local protocols like Zigbee, Thread with Matter, Bluetooth, and my own wired Ethernet network.

## How it adds up

That's the rundown of how this hobby gets out of hand, and why someone might end up building a homelab without ever deciding to. Mine happened organically, one limitation at a time.

# One Screen for All My Background Coding Agents

URL: https://jcosta.tech/writing/fleetview-agent-roster/
Author: John Costa
Published: 2026-10-29

I run a lot of coding agents in the background, and I kept losing track of them. I'd miss which session was waiting on a question, which one had finished, and which one was stuck on a permission prompt.

Claude Code solves this with agent view, a roster of every background session and what each one needs from you. Agent view only exists inside Claude Code, though, and at work I use a GitHub Copilot seat.

So I built [fleetview](https://github.com/costajohnt/fleetview), a port of agent view that puts sessions from [opencode](https://opencode.ai), Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot CLI on one screen. It's one of a set of tools I build for working with agents. fleetview runs several agents at once, and [simon-dash](https://github.com/costajohnt/simon-dash), a local dashboard for my Jira cards and pull requests, shows me what they produce.

![fleetview roster](/assets/post-images/fleetview-agent-roster/demo.gif)

## What it does

fleetview is a live roster of your sessions with an input at the bottom. Type a task there and press enter to start a new session. Sessions are grouped by state, with the ones that need input on top, then the ones working, then the completed ones. Each row shows the session's latest output or the prompt it's waiting on, built without a model call, plus its PR number if its branch has one.

To jump into a session, click its row or arrow down to it and press enter. You land inside the session itself, and `^z` takes you back to the roster (in opencode, `←` on an empty prompt works too).

## Close it whenever you want

Closing or interrupting fleetview never stops a background session. Each session runs as its own process and the roster is saved to disk, so reopening fleetview brings back every session, including the ones that kept working while it was closed. You never have to remember an id to resume something later.

## Every task gets its own worktree

A task started inside a git repository gets its own worktree and branch before the session begins, whichever of the three CLIs runs it. Several agents can work in one repository without touching each other's files, and you merge each branch when its work is done.

## How it compares to agent view

fleetview copies agent view's state groups, most of its keys, its single input box, and its worktree isolation, and the docs note where it differs.

opencode sessions get every feature, including answering a session's questions and permission prompts from the roster, because they run on opencode's server. Claude Code and Copilot sessions run as headless jobs that fleetview watches from outside, so you attach to them to answer anything they ask.

`fleetview --json` reports every session's state with the same words as `claude agents --json`, so scripts written for agent view can read it too, and `fleetview bg "<prompt>"` starts an opencode session from any terminal. When fleetview starts the opencode server, it protects it with a random password, since that server can run shell commands.

## Try it

```
npx fleetview
```

That runs it without installing, and `npm i -g fleetview` installs it. It needs Node 24 or newer on macOS or Linux, plus at least one of opencode, Claude Code or Copilot CLI. opencode unlocks the most features, but the roster runs on Claude Code or Copilot alone. At work I run it both ways, through opencode with Copilot as the model provider and with Copilot CLI sessions directly. The browse view (`^b`) lists every opencode project and session you already have.

fleetview is at version 0.10.0 under the [ISC license](https://github.com/costajohnt/fleetview/blob/main/LICENSE). If you run several agents at once, tell me what's missing in the [issues](https://github.com/costajohnt/fleetview/issues).

# The Era of Rust Rewrites

URL: https://jcosta.tech/writing/era-of-rust-rewrites/
Author: John Costa
Published: 2026-10-25

At Rails World in September, DHH said he hates Rust "with a passion." Then he announced HEY's backend is moving to it. Agents write the code, he doesn't read it, and the new backend needs 99% less CPU and 95% less memory. This from the person who spent twenty years arguing that developer happiness beats CPU cycles.

The reason is cost. Rust has been the answer for slow tools for years, and Ruff and uv proved users will switch for the speed. But learning the language and writing all that verbose code took months, paid up front, before you knew anyone would use it. Most rewrites never justified the bill.

Agents changed the bill. A rewrite takes days now, with the original program as the spec. That makes rewriting slow, popular tools in Rust an arbitrage.

## rbcop

So I rewrote RuboCop, the linter almost every Ruby project runs. rbcop is a drop-in replacement with the same config, command line and output. [nitrocop](https://github.com/6/nitrocop) has chased the same idea since February. rbcop's bet is exact output, full autocorrect and a gem you can install today.

Agents ported all 613 of RuboCop's rules in about nine hours. Getting the output identical took two more days, and hardening it for release took two weeks.

## The speed

In CI with a cold cache, rbcop is about 14 times faster than `rubocop --parallel`.

| Codebase | `rubocop --parallel` | rbcop |
|---|---:|---:|
| rails | 51 s | 2.6 s |
| discourse | 141 s | 10.2 s |
| mastodon | 61 s | 6.1 s |

## The real cost

Agents made the code cheap. Checking it set the pace.

An agent that's wrong sounds exactly like one that's right, so every port and every fix had to match the real RuboCop before it merged. Across nine large codebases, that's about two million offenses and zero differences.

That's what makes a rewrite safe now. The best candidates are slow, widely used tools you can run side by side with your own. There are plenty of them.

---

*rbcop is MIT licensed and [on GitHub](https://github.com/costajohnt/rbcop). Add `gem "rbcop", require: false` and run `bundle exec rbcop`, or use `costajohnt/rbcop@v0.1.2` in GitHub Actions. If it disagrees with RuboCop anywhere, that's a bug, and I want the issue.*

*rbcop is a port of RuboCop, created by Bozhidar Batsov. Its cops, messages and default config are his and RuboCop's contributors' work, used under the MIT license.*

---

# The Job Search Where I Never Applied

URL: https://jcosta.tech/writing/the-job-search-where-i-never-applied/
Author: John Costa
Published: 2026-07-27

Interviewing as a software engineer has never had a real playbook. The process is different at every company, it is genuinely hard on both sides of the table, and the one thing the industry has mostly standardized on, the LeetCode-style algorithm round, won that spot by being objective and easy to compare across candidates, even though it is an artificial test with very little connection to the actual work.

I have job-searched the normal way before, and I knew what that playbook returned. Cold applications disappeared into silence, no reply, no rejection, nothing. Referrals did better, they got me into rooms, but the rooms ended in interviews that ended in nothing. And the track record was only half of it. Cold-applying into silence is quietly demoralizing, every unanswered application chips away at you a little, and grinding LeetCode is a kind of studying I have never enjoyed. What I remember most is that the whole process left me feeling worse every week I kept it up.

So this time I tried close to the opposite. I did not grind LeetCode, and I did not send a single cold application. Since the start of the year I have had real conversations with six companies, every one of them inbound, and two of them became offers.

## The bet

The bet was simple to state and slow to execute. Instead of preparing to look good in interviews, I would spend months **being visibly good at the actual work, in public**, where anyone could see it.

What made the bet easy to commit to was that it paid off no matter what happened. Writing essays, contributing to open source, building things in public, all of it makes me a better engineer and leaves something real behind, whether or not it ever turned into a single interview. I was choosing a path that was good for my career in the worst case, and that I genuinely enjoyed doing. If the search produced nothing, I would still have spent that time getting better at the thing I do. The offers were the upside. They were not the point.

Concretely that meant a few things. I wrote roughly an essay a week, about two dozen of them so far this year, on engineering and AI and the things I was actually doing. I built in the open, which this year came to [146 merged pull requests across 45 repositories](/contributions.html), including projects like Ink and Homebrew and Directus, real codebases with real maintainers and real review standards. I built [a personal site that updates itself](/writing/your-portfolio-site-deserves-a-pipeline/), so every new essay and every new contribution shows up without me touching it, and the site is never stale. I posted on LinkedIn here and there, lightly.

And there was a piece of standard advice I skipped completely. I never asked my network for referrals, even though working your contacts is the first thing everyone tells you to do.

## Spending the leverage

There is a second half to this that matters as much as the visibility, which is that being visible gave me leverage, and I spent the leverage on being selective.

I was deliberate about the kind of interview process I would say yes to. I steered toward work trials, architecture discussions, and take-home challenges, the formats where you do something close to the real job, and I declined loops built around LeetCode-style algorithm rounds. When the inbound interest is steady, you do not have to accept every format. You can pick.

I was also deliberate about which companies. I targeted companies that allow and actively champion AI-assisted development, because that is the work I want to do, and I am not interested in going back to coding the manual way. That filter cut the field down fast, and it cut it in a direction I actually cared about.

## What came back

There were six of these conversations all told, and every one of them started as an inbound contact, a recruiter or a referral that found me. Zero of them started with an application I sent.

It was not fast, and that turned out not to matter, because the inbound was never the number I was watching. For the first few months almost nothing came in. I was doing this work because it made me better and I enjoyed it, and the inbound interest growing was a side effect I had not planned on. If it had never come at all, the time still would not have been wasted. I would have gone into a proactive search, cold applications and all, with a real body of work to point to instead of starting from nothing.

Then the inbound did start, slowly, and then steadily. Of the six conversations, one company passed on me after a first round, which is a normal and healthy thing to have in a funnel and I am mentioning it on purpose. Two of them ended in offers. One came from a recruiter who found me, and the other, the one I accepted, came from a former colleague. We had worked well together, we had kept in touch since, and when a role came up that he thought suited me, he was the one who reached out. That relationship was the whole reason the conversation happened.

## Walking through the door

The visibility opened the doors. Walking through them still took work, and I had a system for that part.

I keep one resume that is genuinely complete. It has everything, every role, every project, the leadership work and the hands-on engineering and the AI work, and it is far too long to send to anyone, five or six pages. It is not a document I submit. It is a source of truth. When a specific role comes up, I use AI to research the company and read the job description closely, then build a tailored resume from it, one or two pages that cherry-picks only the experience that matters for that role.

I also built a small set of strong stories over the course of the process, the kind that can be aimed at different roles depending on what each one needs, and I practiced them until they were smooth. Before each conversation I researched the people I would be talking to and the company itself, so the questions I asked were good ones.

None of that is novel on its own. What made it work was that the door was already open before I started preparing. Preparation is a much better use of energy when it is not also carrying the job of getting noticed.

## The part I did not plan

This is the part I would keep if I had to throw the rest away.

Spending months writing, contributing to open source, and building things in public is not a job-search tactic that sits on top of your real job and competes with it for time. It is the same activity as getting better at the work itself. Reading unfamiliar codebases well enough to contribute to them, explaining your thinking clearly enough to publish it, shipping work that strangers will judge, that is just practice, and the practice compounds.

I felt it at my current job. The contributing and the writing made me a better engineer, which I expected. What I did not expect is that building my own projects, where I had to decide what was worth making and why, made me sharply more product-minded, and that fed straight into the product side of my role. In the same months I was doing all of this, I was exceeding expectations, and I was promoted. I did not split my attention between my job and my job search and do both at half strength. The thing I was doing for one turned out to be the thing that improved the other.

## What I actually think this means

I want to be careful about how I land this, because I am not trying to tell anyone how to run their search. This is one person, one search, one result. The interview format I avoided works fine for plenty of people, and my slow inbound ramp could just as easily have stayed slow.

But the reframe is the part I believe in. A job search is usually a frantic, separate project you spin up when you need it and shut down when it is over. What I tried instead was **being continuously legible**, doing visible work all the time, so that there was nothing to spin up. The search stopped being an event. It became a side effect of the work I was already doing. And the next time I want to move, the work will already be done, because it is the same work.

## The habit stuck

A month into the new job, and none of it has stopped. I am still writing at close to a weekly cadence, still contributing to open source, still building more side projects than I can finish. None of it is a search anymore. It just became how I work.

Part of that is how much fun it is to build with AI tools right now. The loop is fast, the ceiling is high, and it is a good time to be making things. But part of it is that the habit took. It stopped being something I decided to do each week and turned into part of my flow, closer to a hobby I can't put down than a plan I am executing.

---

# The AI Says It's Done. Make It Prove It.

URL: https://jcosta.tech/writing/the-ai-says-its-done/
Author: John Costa
Published: 2026-07-21

What I want from a coding agent is to hand off a real piece of work and trust it gets done without me watching. The agents I use are most of the way there. They write good code, and they can already handle the basic agentic tasks. They can test changes on the command line or in the browser. What's missing is reliability across a long list. When I hand off a ten-step job, I need all ten steps done, not just the first six.

The failure mode that blocks that is laziness.

I hit it building something that runs a multi-step job end to end. The kind of work that's a whole sequence rather than a single task: plan it, write it, test it, review it, carry it through to a finished, verified change. A lot of steps, some with their own inner loops.

The first version was one big prompt describing the whole workflow, and it was lazy in a consistent way. It did the fun part, the implementation, really well. Then it stopped. It wrote the code, decided the interesting work was over, and reported back as if it were done. The manual testing didn't happen. The PR didn't get opened. The whole tail of the workflow, the tedious parts that matter, evaporated, and the summary said "complete."

That's the shape of it. The agent front-loads the parts that look like accomplishment and abandons the parts that feel like cleanup, and the longer the workflow, the more reliably it happens. It's rational behavior. Declaring the work done is what ends the turn, so the agent reaches for that as soon as it plausibly can. If the only thing between "implemented" and "done" is the agent's own say-so, it will round up every time.

So the question stopped being how do I get a smarter agent, and became how do I stop trusting the agent's report about its own work. The answer: take control flow away from the model and give it to a deterministic state machine. The workflow becomes a fixed pipeline the agent is walked through one phase at a time, and no run reaches "done" until every phase has been verified.

## The agent doesn't get to decide it's done

Most agentic setups hand the model the whole job and let it drive. Here's the workflow, here's a long context, go. The agent decides which step it's on, when a step is finished, and when the whole thing is finished. That's the arrangement that lets it stop after the implementation, because stopping is a decision and the decision is the agent's to make.

My setup inverts that. The pipeline is a fixed sequence of phases:

```
preview → plan → implement → quality → test → ship → ci
```

A deterministic orchestrator, plain Go with no model anywhere in the loop, owns the transitions. The agent only ever runs the current phase. "Advance" and "done" are the orchestrator's moves, not the agent's. There's no prompt it can write to jump to done, because done isn't something the agent can say. It's a state the orchestrator moves into, and only after every prior gate has passed.

The allowed transitions are an explicit table the runner checks on every move, and anything that isn't on it is rejected outright. So the ordering is structural: implement can't happen before plan, ship can't happen before the tests ran, and the agent can't route around any of it. Completeness and order come by construction, not by asking nicely in a prompt.

## A deterministic gate between every state

Owning the transitions is half of it. The other half is what happens at each boundary. Before advancing out of a phase, the orchestrator runs a gate: a deterministic check that the phase produced what it was supposed to. The agent reporting `success` is a claim, and a claim doesn't move the machine. Evidence moves the machine.

The gates are boring on purpose:

- The **plan** phase is supposed to leave a plan document. The gate checks `plan.md` exists and isn't empty. No file, no advancing, whatever the agent says.
- The **implement** phase is supposed to write code and a test. The gate checks the diff is non-empty and the test file is in it, then the orchestrator re-runs the test itself and checks for exit zero. The agent doesn't get to tell you the tests pass. The machine runs them.
- The **ci** phase is supposed to end green. The gate re-runs `gh pr checks` and reads the result directly. A red check is red no matter how confident the agent sounded.

There's a subtle version of this I got wrong first. One gate re-ran the test command the agent declared it had used, which sounds airtight until you notice the agent picks the command. Nothing stopped it from declaring `true` as its test and passing the gate honestly. A check that takes its input from the thing it's checking is theater, so the gate now rejects a no-op command before it ever runs.

That's the whole answer to "it claims it's done when it isn't." The claim stops being load-bearing. If the artifact isn't there, the machine stops. If the tests don't pass when the orchestrator runs them, the machine stops. Self-report is demoted from verdict to hint.

And when a gate fails, it fails closed. No silent fallback waves a stuck phase through. A failed gate routes to a terminal failure state that writes a report saying exactly where it stopped and why. A halt you can see beats a "success" you can't trust.

## Fresh context per phase, on purpose

Breaking the workflow into phases bought me a clean answer to context management. Each phase runs as its own fresh process. The `implement` phase doesn't inherit the transcript of the `plan` phase. It boots cold and reads what it needs from disk, the spec, the plan, the artifacts earlier phases left behind, then writes its own result to a small file the next phase reads.

The state machine gives you the seams to do this, because the boundaries between phases are also the boundaries between contexts, and the artifacts on disk are the handoff. Nothing carries the whole history forward in one ballooning window, which is where models lose the thread and start calling half-done work finished. A short context keeps the agent honest: the agent running the `test` phase only knows it's running the test phase, so it can't get complacent about all the good work upstream, because from where it sits, none of it happened.

The inner loops work the same way. The review step runs several fresh reviewers at once, each looking through a different lens, spawned as subagents, their findings merged back deterministically. Each gets a clean read instead of a context already primed to believe the code is fine. The second read is worth more when it genuinely is a second read.

I should be honest about where this reaches its limit. Re-running a test is a fact I can check completely, and no amount of agent confidence changes the exit code. Whether a review was any good is judgment, and there the loop can only prove it ran and converged, not that it was insightful. That part is a probabilistic defense, and I'd rather name it as one than let it ride on the credibility of the checks that are actually guaranteed.

## Why a state machine

You could try to solve laziness with a stern prompt. "Don't claim the tests pass unless you ran them. Don't skip review. Verify before you assert." I've written those prompts. They help a little and fail constantly, because they ask the thing that wants shortcuts to please not take them.

There's a fair objection to all this. Maybe the agent stops early because it was never handed a precise definition of done, and a clear finish line would fix it without any of this machinery. I think that's half right, and it's the reason the machinery works. The gates are the finish line. What matters is where that line lives. If done is something the agent grades itself against, it will always find a reading of the task where it's already there. So the definition has to sit outside the agent, owned by something that isn't trying to end the turn, and enforced by re-running the work instead of re-reading the agent's summary of it. A finish line only the agent can see is just a suggestion.

The state machine works because it doesn't ask. The agent can want to skip the test all it likes; the orchestrator runs the test itself before advancing, so wanting to skip it accomplishes nothing. You stop arguing with the model's incentives and build a structure where the shortcuts aren't reachable.

That's the thesis. Deterministic control flow, deterministic gates, evidence instead of claims. The agent still does the creative work, writing the code, which is what it's genuinely good at. It just doesn't get to be the judge of whether it finished.

Underneath all of it, the thing I was actually after is altitude. Once I can trust a handed-off job to run to completion, I stop needing to sit in the diff watching it happen. I can spend attention on what the work should be instead of whether it got done. Reliable completion is the unlock. The state machine is just how I bought it.

---

# What I Built with Claude Fable 5

URL: https://jcosta.tech/writing/what-i-built-with-claude-fable-5/
Author: John Costa
Published: 2026-07-07

Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5, the first model in a new tier that sits above Opus. I got a window of heavy access to it, and instead of handing it tickets I handed it everything I own. This is a show and tell of what came out of it.

What makes it different is altitude. The models before it were already excellent executors. Fable is the first one that felt clearly better at the level above that. It plans well, it keeps track of a sprawling amount of state without losing the plot, and it dispatches subagents to implement parts of its own plan while it stays at the system level. It also surfaced problems and feature ideas in my projects that passes with Opus and Sonnet never mentioned. That's a qualitative read, and it held up across project after project.

## The audit sweep

The first thing I did was point it at eight of my repos and my whole homelab in a single recon pass: bugs, security issues, refactor opportunities, feature ideas, test gaps, ranked by severity and effort. The output was one worklist with 178 findings. Among them: a failing drive in the media server whose backup chain was already silently broken behind it, and live credentials sitting in unpushed commits on an old project. Both surfaced unprompted.

## The fix wave

Fable wrote the plans and dispatched execution to cheaper models: nine merged PRs across five repos plus a new npm release. The homelab came out more robust, with backups hardened and verified, the disk watchdog re-armed, dead entities cleaned out of Home Assistant, and a handful of security posture fixes.

My little trading system got the most interesting single result. Fable designed its first proper walk-forward out-of-sample test, and the test revealed that the parameters running live were the worst of the candidates. The config got replaced with the one the data blessed. I trusted the test it built, which is a very different thing from trusting the model's own judgment.

## Murmur

I also wanted to see what it could do greenfield, so I built [Murmur](https://github.com/costajohnt/murmur), a local dictation app for macOS, in one session, with the usual arrangement flipped: Opus held the plan and Fable subagents did the typing. It's a small floating pill at the bottom of the screen: click, talk, and the transcript lands at your cursor in whatever app you're in. Transcription runs on the Neural Engine, optional cleanup runs through a local LLM, and nothing ever leaves the machine. v1.0.0 is public and MIT licensed.

I talk to my coding agents constantly, and I wanted the speech-to-text leg of that loop as local and private as the rest of my setup.

## prlore

[prlore](https://github.com/costajohnt/prlore) mines a repo's PR review history into an AGENTS.md conventions file, so the tribal knowledge buried in old review threads becomes something a coding agent can read. Fable drove the v0.3.0 quality release: floors so one-off review trivia can't become a rule, penalties for rules too repo-specific to travel, deduplication, and tiered output for big repos. On one large OSS repo, that turned a 44KB monolith into a 31KB root file plus five small per-area files.

## What I couldn't do before

A lot of this I could not have pulled off a month ago. The earlier models wrote perfectly good code, but they lost the thread on anything this sprawling. Fable held it. It kept a whole worklist, a homelab, and a handful of repos in its head at once, decided what mattered, and handed the busywork down to cheaper models. The expensive model is worth it for judgment and orchestration; most of the work below that line runs fine without it.

All of it ran on the [same setup](https://jcosta.tech/writing/always-on-claude-home-lab-node/) I've written about before: the skills and instructions that guide the agents, the [persistent memory](https://jcosta.tech/writing/how-i-give-claude-code-a-persistent-brain-in-obsidian/) they share across sessions, and now a local voice loop to drive it. Fable took the whole thing as it was and used it better than anything before it.
